text:
1. The destruction of Palestine is breaking the world View image in fullscreen Illustration: Nicolás Ortega/The Guardian “Israel’s war in Gaza,” wrote Moustafa Bayoumi for Guardian US’s weekend featured essay, “is chipping away at so much of what we – in the United States but also internationally – had agreed upon as acceptable, from the rules governing our freedom of speech to the very laws of armed conflict. It seems no exaggeration to say that the foundation of the international order of the last 77 years is threatened by this change in the obligations governing our legal and political responsibilities to each other.” Read more

2. ‘The vehicle suddenly accelerated with our baby in it’: the terrifying truth about why Tesla’s cars keep crashing View image in fullscreen Illustration: Carl Godfrey/The Guardian Elon Musk is obsessive about the design of his supercars, right down to the disappearing door handles. But a series of shocking incidents – from drivers trapped in burning vehicles to dramatic stops on the highway – have led to questions about the safety of the brand. Why, asked Sönke Iwersen and Michael Verfürden, won’t Tesla give any answers? Read more

3. The life swap dream – or a marketing gimmick? The Italian towns selling houses for €1 View image in fullscreen Foreign visitors eye a potential bargain in Sambuca di Sicilia. Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The Guardian If you could move anywhere, where would it be? It’s a question that gestures toward a life in some stage of calcification – the could implying constraint, limitations, the presumption that one simply cannot, in fact, up and move. The €1 house programme serves as the doorway for just this sort of yearning for something new. Hate your job? Want to move but can’t afford a house? Worried about where you’ll retire, or how you’ll even manage to retire at all? If you have the right passport and enough money, you can find somewhere else to live. Why not make that place Italy? Last summer, Lauren Markham and her husband stuffed an inordinate amount of belongings into a preposterous number of bags and flew with their 11-month-old to Italy for an adventure in pursuit of the possibility of a new life. Did they find one? Read more

4. The radical 1960s schools experiment that created a whole new alphabet – and left thousands of children unable to spell View image in fullscreen Judith Loffhagen, who was taught to read using the ITA alphabet. Photograph: Thomas Duffield/The Guardian Decades ago, a generation of UK schoolchildren unwittingly took part in an initiative aimed at boosting reading skills – with lasting consequences. Emma Loffhagen’s mum was one of them. “Throughout my life,” she wrote, “my mum has always been a big reader. She was in three or four book clubs at the same time. She’d devour whatever texts my siblings and I were studying in school, handwrite notes for our lunchboxes and write in her diary every night. Our fridge door was a revolving display of word-of-the-day flashcards. Despite this, she also was and remains, by some margin, the worst speller I have met.” Read more

5. My father, the fake: was anything he told me actually true? View image in fullscreen Michael Briggs. Photograph: Courtesy of Joanne Briggs Growing up in the 1960s, Joanne Briggs knew that her father, Michael, wasn’t like other dads. Once a Nasa scientist, now a big pharma research director, he would regale her and her brother with the extraordinary highlights of his working life. But, wrote Anita Chaudhuri, the well-known scientist was also a fantasist. When his daughter Joanne began digging into his past for a memoir, new lies kept emerging ... Read more
rewritten:
This weekend, we’ve lined up a stellar collection of articles for you to sink your teeth into. From explosive insights on Tesla's hidden dangers to the Italian towns practically giving away homes, there’s something here to pique every interest.

1. Unraveling Palestine: In a thought-provoking piece by Moustafa Bayoumi featured in Guardian US, he warns us how Israel's military actions in Gaza are rewriting global norms and threatening long-standing international agreements—ones we've counted on since WWII.

2. Tesla Terrors: When it comes to safety queries about his luxury cars' alarming mishaps—including terrifying incidents with stuck doors and highway halts—Elon Musk stays tight-lipped, say Sönke Iwersen and Michael Verfürden as they delve into these recurring mysteries around Teslas gone rogue.

3. A Dream or Déjà Vu? Lauren Markham narrates her escapade moving across continents with an infant in tow as she explores Italy’s tempting €1 home initiative that promises fresh beginnings without financial strain—but does reality match the dream?

4. Spelling Sabotage from the 60s: Rewind several decades when schools launched an experimental reading program leaving thousands like Emma Loffhagen’s mum—a literary enthusiast despite being plagued by spelling woes—to cope with unintended lifelong quirks.
